newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr 1-1/2 cents richer, wants more.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr 1-1/2 cents richer, wants more.

text.p: The Australian dollar finished the week 1-1/2 cents richer and on the hunt for more as Japanese investors joined a worldwide re-appraisal of the currency.

It had been under corrective pressure for much of the week after shooting up to a two-month peak of US$0.7912 on Monday but all the profit-taking was absorbed by US$0.7835 support. That encouraged U.S. bank and fund demand, joined by a burst of buying out of Tokyo today which surprised a square market.
The squeeze lifted it to US$0.7900 resistance and dealers reckoned the strength of demand, coupled with the fact that much of it came from Tokyo, boded well for a push higher next week.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the local currency had pushed to US$0.7893/98 from an early US$0.7863/68 and US$0.7845/50 late here Thursday.
The offshore bounce came as a German bank bought up AUD/mark after a dismal set of German unemployment data reinforced the view rates would be stuck near record lows for months to come.
That helped it close near five year highs at 1.3548/62 marks from 1.3471/85 Thursday and, for similar reasons, at 1.1701/17 Swiss francs from 1.1632/48.
The bout of Japanese buying saw it rally to 95.60/70 yen from an early 95.20/30 and past Thursday's 95.51/61.

The demand even prompted whispers the Japanese might be about to rediscover their appetite for yen/A$ dual currency samurai bonds which had waned dramatically since the last cut in official Australian rates on December 11.
Dealers said there was no sign of an actual bond as yet but noted a recent sharp rise in bond yields and money market rates here might well be reviving interest in the A$.

The currency's recoil from US$0.7910 this week was attributed by some to a sharp fall in gold price following news the Swiss central bank planned to sell part of its gold reserves over a 10-year period.
Fluctuations in gold are often linked to moves in the AUD on the premise the yellow metal is a major Australian export and U.S. funds see the A$ as an indirect way of riding gold trends.

Older hands, however, say gold has not really been influential since the 1980s and aspects like long term trends in commodity prices, particularly base metals, and interest differentials have become far more important.

A study of the near-mythical relationship by Westpac found little positive correlation between moves in the gold price and the dollar but a much stronger link between the currency and the Reserve Bank's commodity price index.
"Correlations between the AUD and individual commodities do not generally show strong relationships, especially for short time frames," said Helen Camp, a senior economist at Westpac.
Only aluminium showed a high average correlation at 0.65 percent while gold barely made 0.1 percent.
Positive correlations did tend to rise when the gold price moved sharply, such as in the period from January to February when it slid from $370 an ounce to under $340.
"But even the peak positive correlations are surprisingly low, and question the conventional wisdom that overnight gold price moves are a reliable guide to AUD moves," said Camp.
Many dealers agreed though they doubted gold would lose its place as a convenient excuse for dollar moves which were largely due to the more prosaic forces of demand and supply.

More important were such longer term influences as the dramatic improvement in Australia's inflation performance and the government's commitment to reparing its deficit problems which should eventually be rewarded by a re-rating of the risk premium for the country's debt.
Expectations of continued upbeat economic dataa nd a steady outlook for domestic interest rates should also help medium term. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
